newsitem.title: USA: Women say U.S. Army sex probe used coercion.
newsitem.headline: Women say U.S. Army sex probe used coercion.

text.p: Five woman soldiers from the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground said on Tuesday investigators tried to coerce them into making statements that they had been raped by higher-ranking soldiers.

"They tried to make me say 'rape' and I would not do it," Pvt. Kathryn Leming, of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, told a news conference at the home of a local representative of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People.

NAACP President Kweisi Mfume, also speaking at the news conference, called for an independent investigation of the issue of sexual harassment in the military, saying civil rights may have been violated in the probe.
"There are possible civil rights violations on behalf of the accusers and the accused that ought to be looked at," Mfume said. "We think that it (the investigation) borders on illegality."
Defence Department officials said they would look into the allegations but denied there was any racial harassment.

Seven male instructors at the base have been charged with rape or other sexual misconduct in a scandal that erupted last year and prompted an Army-wide investigation into sexual harassment. Two of the seven took early discharge in lieu of court-martials, while the other five were awaiting trial.
Local NAACP officials have said a prevalence of blacks among the accused and white women among the accusers raised concerns of discrimination.

Pvt. Toni Moreland told the news conference she had falsely stated she had consensual sex with an instructor because investigators told her he would escape punishment if she made the statement. She said she retracted the statement 10 days later after consultation with a chaplain.

Moreland faces a court-martial for making a false statement. Army officials said last week, when her retraction first became public, that the sergeant who was the object of the allegations had not been charged.
The other women said they had resisted investigators' attempts to get them to say they had been raped by targets of the probe. One of the soldiers has been formally charged, they said.

Lt. Col. Gabriel Riesco, chief of staff of the proving ground's Ordnance Centre and School, said none of the statements to investigators by the women who spoke Tuesday had contained allegations of rape. He said the women would not be subject to retribution for their comments Tuesday.
He also denied there was a racial element to the case.
"Race has never been an issue in this investigation," he said. "This is an issue about sin, not about skin."

In Washington, the Defence Department said the allegations by the women would be investigated but denied that the harassment cases were racially motivated or that excessive pressure was brought on women by Army investigators.

"(Army) Secretary (Togo) West told me that he will look very closely at these charges but it is not his belief that the investigators pressured women into making statements," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.

The Army's Criminal Investigation Command later issued a statement saying investigators had used standard procedures in interviewing more than 900 women who had trained at Aberdeen after January 1995 and others who had called in complaints to a sexual-harassment hotline.

Those procedures included advising interview subjects of their legal rights, and requiring that statements be accompanied by a signed affirmation that the statements were made without coercion or threat.
The women who spoke Tuesday said they were given promises ofimmunity or transfers that were not honoured or were told current assignments could be endangered if they did not cooperate.

"Something really wrong is happening," Pvt. Darla Hornberger from Oklahoma said. "I told the truth in my statement. That's not the truth they wanted to hear ... I still refused to say that I was raped."
